newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss pull welcome mat from under Mobutu.
newsitem.headline: Swiss pull welcome mat from under Mobutu.

text.p: Switzerland on Monday denied a visa to Zaire's ailing ruler Mobutu Sese Seko in a calculated snub.

A foreign ministry spokesman said Mobutu, 66, who underwent more than two months of cancer treatment in Lausanne and left on November 4 for the French Riviera where he has a villa, had applied for a new visa but his request had been turned down.
"There was a new request (from Mobutu) for a visa. This request will not be accepted. A visa will not be granted," spokesman Hans Ruedi Bortis told Reuters.

"From the point of view of the Swiss foreign ministry, with the departure of Mr Mobutu, the medical reason for a new visa does not exist any more. We do not have to explain further why we do not issue a new visa," he said.

The rejection of a new visa for Mobutu, banned from much of Western Europe and the United States, has put him on the list of "undesirables" in Switzerland such as Nigeria's military ruler General Sani Abacha.

Mobutu's prolonged absence from Zaire has raised fears that his vast central African country may disintegrate following a successful Tutsi revolt in the east, which has uprooted one million Rwandan Hutu refugees.
Mobutu said last week that he intended to return to Lausanne for a medical check-up.

Zaire's Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, who visited Mobutu at the weekend in France, said on Saturday that he expected the president to meet his doctor during the second half of the month before returning to Zaire.
Swiss official sources said Mobutu applied for a new visa on Friday to return to Switzerland.
During his stay in Switzerland, Mobutu was like an unwanted guest who stayed too long.
His presence added to the image problems of the neutral Alpine country accused by Jewish lobby groups of cosying up to the Nazis during World War Two.

It sparked protests from deputies in Lausanne who appealed to the government to block Mobutu's return and from Zairean exiles in Switzerland who took to the streets of serene Lausanne to demonstrate against his presence.
Privately, Swiss police and other officials breathed a sigh of relief when he packed up.

But there may be sad faces at Lausanne's palatial Beau-Rivage Hotel on the shores of Lake Geneva, where Mobutu and his entourage were favourite clients. They were reported to have paid nearly a million Swiss Francs ($785,000) in total for their luxury suites.
His aides have repeatedly said Mobutu plans to return soon to Zaire, but he has appeared weak and thin during his few public appearances.
During his stay in France, Mobutu received U.N. envoy Raymond Chretien, Congo President Pascal Lissouba and South African Vice-President Thabo Mbeki.
In Lausanne, Swiss secrecy and discreet security surrounded the Zairean strongman, whose visitors included France's former Interior Minister Charles Pasqua.
